processing: Holly shoots and leaves are heated to stop browning and then dried. Sticky leaf makes this step hard to do evenly, and one Hainan research institute has used microwave heating to solve it.
harvest_season: Picking seasons for the Hainan leaf are little recorded; young shoots and leaves are the usual raw material for kuding.
appearance_dry: Dark green, waxy-looking leaves, as is typical of holly kuding, either twisted or in strips.
appearance_liquor: Green shading into yellow, clear and bright.
appearance_wet: Thick, waxy green leaves that hold their shape, as is typical of holly kuding.
taste_profile: Waxy-leaved and fresh, with a fairly light bitterness that gives way to a strong sweet return. It stands up to many infusions.

brewing.notes: Use far less than you would of tea. Too much leaf or too long a steep is the usual mistake, and turns it harshly bitter.

vintage_note: Sold as recent stock without a vintage year, as is usual for kuding; no market for aged lots is established. Keep it dry and drink within a year or two. Check that it is the holly type, since the name kuding covers several plants across China.
description:
Hainan kuding is a bitter leaf tisane from a holly, not from the tea plant. Its raw material grows in the tropical forest of the Wuzhishan area, and promoters speak of very old trees. The word kuding means roughly bitter nail, and it covers several unrelated plants in China, so the holly species is the point here.

The shoots are heated and dried in a way borrowed from green tea, though the sticky leaf makes even heating difficult. That is why a Hainan research institute has worked on microwave heating. The result is a waxy, durable leaf that gives colour for many rounds.

For a kuding, it is often described as light in its bitterness and strong in its sweet aftertaste. The liquor is green-yellow and clear. Start with a small pinch, keep steeps short, and add time slowly, because even a little too much leaf can overwhelm the cup.

Ask which plant you are buying, and whether the leaf is really from Hainan rather than from the larger kuding growing areas of the mainland. Sellers make strong claims about blood pressure, lipids and blood sugar, and it is better to buy it as a bracing, bitter-sweet drink.
history:
Little is documented about when the Hainan leaf entered regular use.

Modern work is clearer: the leaf is now covered in Hainan's tea promotion, alongside the Chengmai kuding that is also promoted on the island, and institutes have worked on improving its processing.
